lesson.title: Why 1789?
lesson.objective: Explain how royal debt, rising bread prices, and ideas about political representation combined to start the French Revolution.
lesson.approachReason: The puzzle of why a long-standing debt crisis erupted in 1789 lets learners uncover each pressure before connecting them.

blocks.heading: Clue 1: The crown needed money
blocks.body:
France's government had borrowed heavily to pay for wars, including its support for the American Revolution. By the late 1780s, repaying debt consumed a large share of its income. Raising more money was difficult: proposed tax reforms met resistance from groups defending their privileges.

After other efforts failed, King Louis XVI summoned the Estates-General, an assembly of representatives, to meet in 1789. A financial problem had opened a national political debate.
blocks.example: The debt was not new in 1789. The chance to argue publicly over how France should be governed was.

hints: What was the king trying to change to raise money?
Think about why people who opposed those changes mattered.
blocks.retry: The king needed a way through a dispute over money and taxes. Calling representatives together also gave them a place to challenge how decisions were made.

blocks.heading: Clue 2: Bread became harder to afford
blocks.body:
A poor harvest in 1788 helped push bread prices upward into 1789. For many families, bread was an essential daily expense, so a price rise could consume money needed for everything else.

The government's debt did not cause the poor harvest. But the two pressures struck at the same time: the crown struggled to raise money while many people struggled to buy food.
blocks.example: A deputy debating taxes and a Parisian trying to buy bread faced different problems—but both had reason to think the situation could not continue.

hints: Focus on what happens to a family's spending when an essential food costs more.
Would a poor harvest directly erase government debt?
blocks.retry: A high bread price matters especially when bread takes up much of a household's budget. It can turn a political crisis into an immediate concern for people who are not in the assembly.

blocks.heading: Clue 3: Who should have a say?
blocks.body:
Ideas about liberty, equality before the law, and government answerable to the nation had circulated before 1789. They gave critics a way to argue that political power should not rest only with the king and privileged groups.

When the Estates-General met, representatives of the Third Estate—the vast majority of French people who were neither clergy nor nobility—pressed for a stronger voice. On June 17, 1789, their deputies declared themselves the National Assembly, claiming to represent the nation.
blocks.example: New ideas did not make bread cheaper or pay the debt. They helped people argue about who had the authority to solve those problems.

hints: Which pressure brought representatives together in 1789?
Then ask what made change urgent outside the assembly and what gave deputies a reason to claim authority.
blocks.retry: Think of three different roles: debt pushed the king to seek a solution, expensive bread sharpened public anger, and political ideas shaped demands for change.

blocks.heading: Why 1789?
blocks.body: No single clue solves the puzzle. Years of debt pushed the king to summon representatives in 1789; soaring bread prices made the crisis urgent for many households; and ideas about representation helped deputies challenge the old political order. Together, these pressures turned a search for money into the beginning of a revolution.
blocks.example: Debt explains the political opening. Bread prices explain much of the urgency. New ideas help explain why the answer became a demand for political change.

activities.title: An old debt, a new crisis
activities.prompt: France had owed money for years. What might make that old problem turn into a national political confrontation in 1789?
activities.reveal: To find a way out of its financial crisis, the king summoned representatives. That created an opening for a much bigger argument—but it does not yet explain why so many people felt the moment was urgent.

options.text: The king's search for new revenue led him to summon representatives, who could challenge his plans.
options.feedback: Yes. The debt created pressure for action, and the assembly created a place for political demands.

options.text: All of France's debt was first borrowed in 1789.
options.feedback: The debt had built up over many years. The puzzle is why it became politically explosive then.

options.text: A poor harvest paid off the government's loans.
options.feedback: A poor harvest could raise food prices; it could not repay government debt.

options.text: The king no longer needed taxes, so he gave up political power.
options.feedback: The government needed more revenue, not less, and the king did not simply give up power.

activities.title: How the pressures met
activities.prompt: Trace the events in order. At which point did the king's money problem become a debate over who could speak for France?
activities.reveal: The debt and the ideas about representation predated 1789. The poor harvest increased hardship, while the meeting of representatives gave political demands a place to take shape.

events.title: War spending adds to debt
events.detail: France's support for the American Revolution adds to an already costly burden of borrowing.

events.title: A poor harvest
events.detail: A poor harvest helps drive bread prices higher into the following year.

events.title: An assembly is called
events.detail: Facing a financial crisis, the king announces that the Estates-General will meet in 1789.

events.title: The Estates-General meets
events.detail: Representatives gather to address the crisis, opening disputes about taxes and political voice.

events.title: Deputies claim to represent the nation
events.detail: Third Estate deputies declare themselves the National Assembly, challenging the old political order.

questions.question: In the late 1780s, the king's advisers need more revenue, but attempts to change taxes face resistance. Why might summoning the Estates-General change the situation?
options: It gives representatives a forum to debate the financial crisis and make their own demands.
It immediately erases the government's debts.
It guarantees that privileged groups will volunteer to pay every tax.
It allows the king to avoid discussing taxes altogether.
questions.correctAnswer: It gives representatives a forum to debate the financial crisis and make their own demands.
questions.explanation: The crown sought a way through its financial crisis. Bringing representatives together also gave them an opportunity to contest how France was governed.

questions.question: In spring 1789, a wage-earning family finds that its usual loaf costs much more than before. Why could this deepen unrest?
options: Bread now takes a larger share of the family's money, making daily life more precarious.
Higher bread prices automatically repay the king's debts.
A bread shortage means no one can discuss politics.
Bread becomes less important to the family's spending.
questions.correctAnswer: Bread now takes a larger share of the family's money, making daily life more precarious.
questions.explanation: Bread was an essential expense for many families. When its price rose, hardship made the wider crisis feel immediate.

questions.question: A Third Estate deputy in June 1789 says the assembly should speak for the nation. Meanwhile, people outside it face expensive bread. Which account best explains why the crisis became revolutionary?
options: Debt brought representatives together, food prices heightened hardship, and ideas about representation supported a challenge to royal authority.
Food prices alone caused the king to borrow money for earlier wars and created every political demand.
New political ideas immediately lowered bread prices and ended the debt crisis.
The king called representatives because France had no financial problems.
questions.correctAnswer: Debt brought representatives together, food prices heightened hardship, and ideas about representation supported a challenge to royal authority.
questions.explanation: The pressures played different, connected roles. A fiscal crisis created the political opening, hardship added urgency, and ideas about representation shaped the challenge.

trace.blocks: activity > explain > check > explain > check > explain > activity > check > explain

problems: The timeline activity asks learners to identify a turning point but provides no way to record or test their choice, so it functions mostly as reading.
Several incorrect options are implausible, making the checks easier than the ideas warrant.
The retry explanations largely restate the lesson rather than offering a genuinely different way to understand the causes.
